newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - Core markets take center stage.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Core markets take center stage.

text.p: The United States and Germany have grabbed the spotlight on the global fixed-income stage, as yield-starved investors return to the core bond markets for value, portfolio managers said.

"Our thinking is that the best relative value over the next several weeks in world bond markets is to be found in the core markets," said Jonathan Francis, head of global strategy at Putnam Investments.
"In Europe that would be Germany. In North America, or the dollar block, that would be U.S. Treasuries," Francis added.

Analysts said a slowing economy with no sign of rising inflation in the Unites States was likely to keep the bond market active in the near future. "The (U.S.) economy is not going to be a threat," Francis said.

Investors have profited handsomely as rates have shrunk in marginal, higher-yielding markets this year, but many are now looking to lock in those gains and get back into more stable assets, analysts said.
"Global investors are overloaded on spread trades ... which are losing some steam," said a portfolio manager at a U.S. investment bank who asked not to be named.
"As we come into the year end I think people will take profits on those trades and look for the (U.S.) Treasury market as a safe place to be for the time being," he added.

Portfolio managers said value in the so-called spread trades have deteriorated in general. But they added that some emerging markets and the high-yielding portion of Europe are seen as particularly affected.
They said countries like Italy, Sweden and Spain, which not too long ago were seen offering solid value, have lost some of their luster when compared to other core markets in Europe.
"Our view is that there's very little value left in the spread trades ... I think those are pretty fully priced," Putnam's Francis said.
Although Japan is also considered a core market, analysts said Japanese bonds are still an uncertain bet.
"On the one hand, it's really difficult to make the case for being long in Japan," the money manager said.
"But on the other hand you don't want to be short either. Maybe a neutral position would be the best place to be for now," he added.
Analysts said a recent advance of the yen against the dollar sent some jitters to the market about the possibility of higher interest rates in Japan.
Jitters about the financial health of some domestic banks, however, have eased fears of an imminent rate hike.
Earlier this week, Japanese authorities ordered a troubled institution, Hanwa Bank, to halt most of its business, the first time it has done so since World War II.
The Oceania block was also seen as an alternative for those investors seeking high returns and willing to tolerate a little bit more risk.
Pundits said Australia and New Zealand are good investment options as their securities remain fairly priced but still show some value left across their yield curves.
"We're seeing value in Australia and New Zealand," said Claude Erb, director of research at First Chicago Investment Management Co, adding he also saw some value in the United Kingdom.
Erb said the reason why he would pick those countries was rather technical.
"There is nothing that really stands out as far as a major catalyst or a major issue with regard with those countries ... It really think it's a money flow sort of story," Erb said.
The economist said that tightening spreads in most European and emerging markets might prompt players to look into alternative ways to invest their money.
"Those seem to be the three countries (U.K., Australia and New Zealand) that were left behind and represent in our mind the best values," Erb said.
-- N.A. Treasuries Desk, 212-859-1676
